title: Attached Foraminifera form plane spirals with whorls flattened on the attached side

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Attached Foraminifera form plane spirals with whorls flattened on the attached side

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Most spiral Foraminifera are plane (discoid) spirals because some force keeps the chambers in a plane, especially in forms that live attached to rock or seaweed, whose whorls are flattened on the attached surface; freely floating forms such as Globigerina tend towards helicoid spirals.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The majority of spiral forms, on the other hand, are plane or discoid spirals, and we may take it that in these cases some force has exercised a controlling influence, so as to keep all the chambers in a plane. This is especially the case in forms like Rotalia or Discorbina (Fig. 316), where the organism lives attached to a rock or a frond of sea-weed

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Types of foraminiferal shell”. Scope: benthic attached versus planktonic Foraminifera

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-08: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.71

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Both habitat and shell geometry have clear modern operational definitions and public sources. Comparative data can test the association, although attributing it specifically to attachment force remains less decisive.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify species by attached benthic versus free planktonic habit and quantify planarity, attached-side flattening and helical displacement from shell scans. Strong habitat-associated differences after phylogenetic and size controls support the claim; no association or opposite patterns refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ecology is correlated with phylogeny and shell construction.

Many species lack public 3D scans.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Coiling geometry and life habit are observable and widely described, and planktonic assemblages are already tabulated globally. No single open table pairs attachment, flattening, and coiling across benthic genera, so the test requires a compilation. Exceptions are informative where they have been illustrated, but phylogenetic structure will keep the result from being a clean mechanical demonstration.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score planispiral versus trochospiral coiling, ventral flattening, and life habit (attached, free benthic, planktonic) across genera, then test the association with a phylogenetic model. The claim is supported if attached species are disproportionately plane and flattened on the attached face while planktonic species are disproportionately helicoid; abundant attached trochospirals or free planispiral plankton would undermine the stated contrast.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Attached versus free habit and the flattened face are not fields in the census databases and must be compiled from monographs.

Coiling mode is phylogenetically conserved, so a habit correlation can be a clade effect.
